Breaking: Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.
  • They’re actually different technologies.
  • In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.

They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate.

In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.

Sources indicate that containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed.

It has been revealed that that different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick.

A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start promptly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead.

This design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way.

ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged.

Docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine.

Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI:.

That creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox.

It has been revealed that coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape.

Sources indicate that an agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment.

Sources indicate that A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, introduces the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind.

Recent findings suggest that A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last.

Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.”.

Sources indicate that the program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, problem descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile.

We’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it.

According to recent reports, put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things:.

The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment.

Industry observers note that the short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker.

Industry observers note that this is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents.

In a recent development, A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them.

ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system.

Sources indicate that docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills.

Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted users because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers.

Industry observers note that an agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved.

It has been revealed that the socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it.

It has been revealed that docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen.

In a recent development, let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this.

Industry observers note that containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it.

Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM.

Needs the host socket or a nested daemon.

Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM.

Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone.

Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies.

Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy.

Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets.

Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services.

Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes.

Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm.

Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems.

Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files.

These controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM.

When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls.

A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention.

In a recent development, the workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox.

MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both.

So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code.

Industry observers note that docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team.

Kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so plan for changes to both.).

The host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository.

Sources indicate that running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would.

Industry observers note that if your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies.

Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary.

Reach for Docker Sandboxes when.

You control the code and its dependencies.

The workload generates or fetches code at runtime.

Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image.

The session accumulates state for hours.

The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it.

The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket.

You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes.

You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off.

The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running.

You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel.

If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes.

Start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows.

Industry observers note that containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup.

Recent findings suggest that docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. Once one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance extends the same controls across your organization.

Give it a try and get a sandbox running with one command. Start with sbx run claude and the Docker Sandboxes quickstart. Recent findings suggest that no. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. A sandbox can run containers, which is why the two are easy to confuse.

Yes. Each sandbox has a private Docker Engine, so the agent can build images, run Testcontainers, and start Compose applications without the host socket or Docker-in-Docker.

In a recent development, no. Containers remain the right tool for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Sandboxes add a stronger boundary for autonomous agents, and containers keep running inside them.

In a recent development, A container isolates a workload. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. A container can be part of containment, and Docker Sandboxes add the microVM boundary an autonomous agent needs.

Docker describes four requirements: containment (a boundary the model can’t rewrite), control (visibility into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it), choice (swapping models, agents, and tools without rebuilding), and capacity (a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine).

cgo's pointer check is all over the place

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

cgo does syntactic transformations unaware of Go types, allowing almost unnoticeable changes in source code to turn a 48ns call into a 76µs call. And its correctness checks can panic on legal code, while being exhaustive and expensive in some cases and lax in others.

In this article, we recap some of the basics of Go's Foreign Function Interface (FFI), cgo, and take a look at example programs that explain its behavior and limits. In particular we'll show how passing the same pointer to C can panic on code that the docs allow, how it can be about 1600x slower depending on how the C call is written, and when the cgo argument checker just gives up.Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing highlighted.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle complications like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we at the moment expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Recent findings suggest that grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing highlighted.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle challenges like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: newly introduced(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field."
