Industry News: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • According to recent reports, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • It has been revealed that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting complications by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

According to recent reports, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

It has been revealed that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting matter by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

According to recent reports, for each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

In a recent development, AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review concerns, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

Sources indicate that I open one of my environments. The Challenges tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

Sources indicate that the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

Sources indicate that the Remediation section highlights a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the concern is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

Industry observers note that the Scans tab reveals the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated concerns in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

It has been revealed that to learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that let’s start with the big picture.
  • But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its fresh brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Sources indicate that let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker.

A newly introduced Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a upcoming way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one significant constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.

Recent findings suggest that together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

In a recent development, on the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Recent findings suggest that agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the fresh Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Industry observers note that trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this substantial alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a newly introduced day for Docker. Something that claims and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

Industry observers note that if you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation tech giant, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

According to recent reports, we’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

In a recent development, wherever this newly introduced era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

Terri Avnaim is the CMO of Docker, where she leads global marketing and shapes the manufacturer’s positioning and go-to-market strategy for the agentic era.

#161244. Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4779 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reiver ↗ Open Full Page

Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reiver

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software.
  • Recent findings suggest that every numbered statement below is false.
  • Industry observers note that these are not made up for effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software. That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles. This article ("Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto") is one of my contributions to that genre.

Recent findings suggest that every numbered statement below is false. Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

Industry observers note that these are not made up for effect. Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

Handles can change. The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it (DIDs) “unique and immutable”.

My handle changed! My handle was first reiver.bsky.social, then became reiver.myatproto.social, and then later became reiver.blacksky.team. You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit. (did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID.).

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Use the DID. Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID's handle is from time to time.

According to recent reports, but, you need to normalize the DID before using it. DIDs are URIs, and URI schemes are case-insensitive (RFC 3986) — so DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz are the same DID. ATProto requires the normalized (lowercase) form: normalize DIDs when they come from user input, store and compare only the normalized form, and reject non-normalized DIDs that arrive in protocol data.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team.

A upcoming handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one. joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine. Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

For example, Bluesky's own account (did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social, and then became bsky.app. You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit. (Another reason to key users by DID, and not by any part of their handle.).

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

A handle can change at any moment. The user can switch to a fresh handle. The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else. Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving. The handle specification says “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”.

So, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it. The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”. Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes. And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID.

In a recent development, an account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it. The DID specification says “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”.

In API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).” And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional. So, your code needs a “no handle” case.

Every handle ends in .bsky.social.

Any Internet domain can be a handle. And, other PDSes hand out their own — the blacksky.app PDS, for example, offers .blacksky.app, .myatproto.social, .cryptoanarchy.network, and others.

Even if a user's handle is not a .bsky.social handle now, their first handle was.

A user's first handle is whatever they got when their account was created — on whichever PDS they signed up with. com.atproto.server.createAccount just takes a “Requested handle for the account”, and each PDS offers its own domains. So, someone who signed up on blacksky.app might start out as alice.myatproto.social — and never have had a .bsky.social handle at all.

You can see this in a DID's audit log on plc.directory (https://plc.directory//log/audit) — the very first operation (the one that created the DID) shows the first handle, and the first PDS. For example, the audit log for did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w (plc.directory/did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w/log/audit) has just 1 operation — the one that created it, on November 13th, 2026. Its first handle was shadowoftruth.myatproto.social, and its first PDS was blacksky.app. It has never had a .bsky.social handle.

A handle is a third-level domain — like alice.bsky.social, alice.blacksky.app, or alice.myatproto.social.

According to recent reports, A handle can have any number of segments, as long as there are at least 2. example.com is a valid handle — and so is apple.banana.cherry.example.com. The handle specification only says “there must be at least two segments” (so a bare top-level domain like com is not allowed), each segment can be 1 to 63 characters, and the whole handle can be at most 253 characters. Its own examples include a.co, 8.cn, and XX.LCS.MIT.EDU; and the official test vectors include john.test.bsky.app, and a valid handle with 10 segments.

Industry observers note that with DNS (a TXT record at _atproto.) or HTTPS (/.well-known/atproto-did). You need to support both.

If a DID document lists a handle, the account owns that handle.

Anyone can put any handle in their own DID document. The handle has to resolve back to the same DID — both directions must agree. Otherwise, show handle.invalid.

com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle checks both directions for you.

Its own lexicon indicates it “Does not necessarily bi-directionally verify against the the DID document.” (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Handles are case-sensitive — so keep the capitalization the user typed.

Handles are not case-sensitive. The handle specification claims “Only normalized (lowercase) handles should be stored in records or used in outbound API calls. Applications should not preserve user-provided case information and attempt to display handles in anything other than lower-case.” Its example: “the handle input string BlueskyWeb.xyz should be normalized, stored, and displayed as blueskyweb.xyz.”.

Recent findings suggest that it is just decoration, for display. The handle specification indicates “Handles may be prefixed with the "at" symbol (like @user.example.com) in user interfaces, but this is not a valid syntax for a handle in records, APIs, and other back-end contexts.” So, strip it from user input before resolving.

On example.com's own site, it is fine to show @alice.example.com as just @alice.

It has been revealed that the handle specification says “Handles should generally not be truncated to local context. For example, the handle @alice.example.com should not be displayed as @alice, even in the local context of an example.com service.” (It also warns that very long handles “can result in similar challenges when truncated at the start or end” — for example, a handle that starts with paypal.com being shown as paypal.com….).

did:web is supported too. Your code needs to handle both.

In ATProto, “did:web is restricted in atproto to only full domains, not paths or port specification” (from the record key specification).

Whatever plc.directory returns for a DID is that DID's document.

Industry observers note that check that the document's id matches the DID you asked for. (See: How-To Resolve a DID to a PDS.).

A did:plc is case-insensitive — so DID:PLC:… or did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR is fine.

The did: and the method name (plc) must be lowercase — “The URI starts with lowercase did:”, and “The method segment is one or more lowercase letters”. And, a did:plc identifier is lowercase too: “the entire identifier is lower-case (and should be normalized to lower-case)” (from the did:plc specification). The ATProto specification says “protocol implementations should reject DIDs with invalid casing.” (plc.directory answered did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR, did:PLC:…, and DID:PLC:… with 400 “Resolution of non-PLC DIDs not supported”.).

(This is about DIDs in protocol data — records, tokens, API responses. As a URI, the did: scheme is case-insensitive, so DID: means the same thing — but ATProto requires the normalized, lowercase form there. DIDs typed in by a user may be normalized; see item 2. And, even under the general DID syntax, the method name must be lowercase, so did:PLC:… is invalid on its own.).

DIDs are case-sensitive — so did:plc:abc… and did:plc:ABC… are 2 different accounts.

In a recent development, for did:plc, the uppercase one is not a different DID — it is not a valid did:plc at all, since its identifier is lowercase-only base32. The ATProto specification indicates “the presently-supported methods are not case sensitive, and could be safely lowercased”, and that “It is permissible to attempt case normalization when receiving user-controlled input, such as when parsing public URL path components, or text input fields.” So: reject bad casing in protocol data; lowercasing what a user typed is fine.

If a DID parser accepts it, it is a valid DID.

Industry observers note that A generic DID parser only checks the generic syntax — which allows uppercase in the identifier (the test vectors list did:method:VAL as valid). The indigo library's syntax.ParseDID accepts did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR — but plc.directory rejects it. Generic syntax is not the same as a valid did:plc.

A did:plc's DID document never changes.

The DID never changes — but its DID document can. Each change is a signed operation, and the handle (alsoKnownAs), the PDS (the #atproto_pds service), the signing key (#atproto), and the rotation keys can all be changed.

For example, my DID's audit log (plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit) has 4 operations:.

And, the did:plc specification has 2 more surprises. A “tombstone” operation “clears all of the data fields and permanently deactivates the DID”. And, there is a 72-hour window during which a higher-authority rotation key can “"rewrite" history”. So, do not cache a DID document forever — re-resolve it from time to time, and watch the firehose for #identity events.

“Personal” Data Server means one server per person.

“Many PDSes will host multiple people” (the glossary). Most host many.

Bluesky owners' data is on bsky.social.

The server a user logs in at is the server that has their data.

It has been revealed that it might be an entryway — a separate OAuth server for many PDSes. puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network's /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource lists https://bsky.social as its authorization server. (blacksky.app, on the other hand, lists itself.).

Sources indicate that accounts can migrate to another PDS — that is a core design goal. Always look up the current PDS from the DID document (and do not cache it forever).

A user's PDS can show them everyone's posts.

According to recent reports, A PDS only has its own accounts' data. For timelines, threads, and counts, it forwards the request to an AppView. (See: ATProto PDS.).

A user's PDS builds (or renders) their timeline.

The timeline (app.bsky.feed.getTimeline) is built by an AppView. The PDS just forwards the app's request to it. And, no server renders it — the AppView returns JSON, and the app (on the user's phone or computer) renders that.

According to recent reports, (This one used to be closer to true. Bluesky's feed generator starter kit still indicates “In the future, the PDS will hydrate the feed with the help of an App View, but for now, the PDS handles hydration itself.” Today, the AppView does it. See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

Bluesky's PDS software is the only PDS software.

Any server that implements the right end-points is a PDS. (For example, the Blacksky team's rsky project, written in Rust, includes rsky-pds.).

Self-hosting a PDS means you have to index the entire network.

A PDS only stores its own accounts' data. Indexing the network is the job of relays and AppViews — a self-hosted PDS uses someone else's. (In Bluesky's PDS software, PDS_CRAWLERS defaults to https://bsky.network, and PDS_BSKY_APP_VIEW_URL defaults to https://api.bsky.app.).

That is why the hardware is small. The official PDS instructions recommend 1 GB of memory, 1 CPU core, and a 20 GB SSD — for 1 to 20 users. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Every record on the network is a Bluesky post.

It has been revealed that A repository can hold records of any type — any lexicon, from any app — all mixed together in the same user's repository. Calendar events, bookmarks, blog posts, game state, workout logs, or a custom app's own schema: each is just another collection. (And, by default, a PDS accepts records whose lexicon it does not know — “optimistic validation”.).

For example, my repository (reiver.blacksky.team) has these collections, according to com.atproto.repo.describeRepo:.

According to recent reports, only one of those 14 collections is Bluesky posts (app.bsky.feed.post). Even among Bluesky's own record types, most are not posts — likes, reposts, follows, lists, a profile. And, actor.rpg.* and equipment.rpg.item are from a different app altogether. (See: ATProto Record.).

Everything a user does on ATProto is public.

Industry observers note that everything in a user's repository is public — posts, likes, follows, and even blocks (see the next item). But, not everything a user does is stored as a record in their repository. For example, in Bluesky:.

Recent findings suggest that note that this data is private from the public — not encrypted. The PDS (or chat service) that holds it can read it. And, these are features of particular apps and services (app.bsky.*, chat.bsky.*), not a privacy guarantee of the protocol itself.

(The spaces proposal would add something fresh: records that only some people may read — see the Spaces section, below.).

Blocks are private, like mutes.

Recent findings suggest that in Bluesky, a mute is private — but a block is a public record. A block is an app.bsky.graph.block record in the blocker's repository, and its lexicon notes so plainly: “Record declaring a 'block' relationship against another account. NOTE: blocks are public in Bluesky; see blog posts for details.”.

So, anyone can list an account's blocks — for example, with com.atproto.repo.listRecords, or from the firehose — and see who blocked whom. If you build features on blocks, treat them as public information.

It has been revealed that the author is the repository the record is in. (See: ATProto Record.).

A record key is unique within a repository.

“The tuple of (did, rkey) is not unique; the tuple (did, collection, rkey) is unique.”.

According to recent reports, TIDs (like 3n2opitxdyc2j) are the most common, but each record type's lexicon claims which kind of record key it uses. The record key specification defines 4 kinds:.

Some other things about record keys:.

A tid record key tells you when the record was created.

“Record keys are "user-controlled data" and may be arbitrarily selected by hostile accounts.” Do not trust them as timestamps.

A record's createdAt is when it was created.

Industry observers note that it is whatever the client put there. The app.bsky.feed.post lexicon describes it as a “Client-declared timestamp”. A client can set it to any time — past or future.

When a record was actually seen is tracked separately, by the services that see it:.

For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts, public.api.bsky.app reported createdAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:36.813Z, and indexedAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:38.543Z — close, here, but nothing requires them to be. (Even these are each one service's view — a different AppView may have indexed it at a different time.).

ATProto JSON is just regular JSON.

It is JSON with extra rules, from the ATProto data model — the same data model that is also written as DRISL-CBOR (the successor to DAG-CBOR) for storing, signing, and hashing. The differences from regular JSON:.

It has been revealed that it is not DAG-JSON either — the data model specification notes ATProto uses $link “as the key name instead of /”. And, there are practical limits too — for example, Bluesky's data validation guide suggests at most 32 levels of nesting, and 1 MiB per record (as CBOR). (See: ATProto Record.).

Records can contain floating-point numbers.

Floats are not allowed in the data model — they do not round-trip reliably, and the bytes must be exact for hashing.

You can compute a record's CID by hashing its JSON.

According to recent reports, the CID is a hash of its DRISL-CBOR encoding. JSON is not byte-exact.

A missing field and a null field mean the same thing.

They are different — and both are different from false, 0, or an empty array.

Every record in a repository is valid against its lexicon.

According to recent reports, by default, a PDS only checks records whose lexicon it knows (“optimistic validation”, or “fail-open”). Validate what you read.

A record with fields its lexicon does not mention is invalid.

Unexpected fields should be ignored — “at worst as warnings”. (Validating a post with an extra mood field against app.bsky.feed.post passes. See: ATProto Lexicon.).

A deleted record leaves a tombstone.

“Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or "tombstone" of previous contents.”.

Deleting a record removes it from the Internet.

Deleting a record removes it from the user's repository. But, by then, copies may already be elsewhere — the creation went out on the PDS's firehose, and relays, AppViews, feed generators, search indexes, backups, and anyone else watching may have kept it.

The deletion goes out on the firehose too, and the specifications expect other services to follow it. The accounts specification says “When accounts remove records from their public repositories, hosting services should remove public access to that content.” And, the sync specification says mirrors should “respect repository updates (eg, record deletion) … in a timely manner (within seconds or minutes)”. But, “should” is not a guarantee — nothing forces every service to comply, and a copy someone else kept (or a screenshot) is out of the user's control.

It has been revealed that (And, since the data was signed, such a copy can still be shown to be genuine. Treat anything written to a public repository as published.).

An NSID is an address you can fetch.

It is a name — a reversed Internet domain plus a name. (See: ATProto NSID.).

It is safe to lowercase an NSID.

The Internet domain part is not case-sensitive, but the name is — getRecord is not getrecord. “Implementations should not force-lowercase NSIDs.”.

Implementations reject an NSID whose Internet domain part is longer than 253 characters.

The specification claims 253 — but the official test vectors list a 283-character one as valid, and Bluesky's TypeScript and Go code only check the 317-character total.

If _lexicon.feed.bsky.app does not exist, try _lexicon.bsky.app.

Lexicon resolution is not hierarchical. If the exact record does not exist, resolution simply fails. (See: How-To Resolve a Lexicon.).

The app.bsky.* lexicons are in the bluesky-social/atproto repository on GitHub.

Not anymore — its main branch has no lexicons/app/bsky/ directory. Resolve them from the network instead (they are published by did:plc:4v4y5r3lwsbtmsxhile2ljac).

A union in a lexicon lists every type you will ever see there.

Recent findings suggest that unions are open by default — fresh types can be added. (The live app.bsky.feed.post lexicon's embed union includes app.bsky.embed.gallery, which older code will not know about.).

It can change — in compatible ways (new optional fields, more union types, etc).

You need a special library to talk ATProto.

Recent findings suggest that XRPC is plain HTTP and JSON. curl works. (See: ATProto XRPC.).

A server returns the error names listed in the end-point's lexicon.

Not always. resolveHandle's lexicon lists HandleNotFound, but public.api.bsky.app answered an unknown handle with InvalidRequest.

The specification itself warns that “many services will return generic load-balancer or reverse-proxy HTML error pages.”.

An end-point a server does not have returns 404.

A Bluesky PDS answered a made-up end-point with 401 AuthMissing.

A cursor means something you can use.

It has been revealed that treat it as opaque. (One server's listRecords cursor happens to be the last record key — do not depend on that.).

In a recent development, every PDS has its own firehose, and there are several relays — for example, Bluesky's bsky.network and the Blacksky team's atproto.africa. (See: ATProto Relay.).

A user's PDS knows who follows them.

Industry observers note that A follow is an app.bsky.graph.follow record — stored in the follower's repository, with the followed account's DID as its subject. So, a user's PDS knows exactly who the user follows, but not who follows them — those records are spread across everyone else's repositories, on every PDS. (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

Likes and replies live on the author's post.

Recent findings suggest that they live in the repositories of the people who liked or replied. A like is an app.bsky.feed.like record in the liker's repository, whose subject is a strong reference (uri and cid) to the post. A reply is an app.bsky.feed.post record in the replier's repository, with a reply field pointing at the thread's root and the parent post. (Reposts work the same way.) The author's post record itself has no list of likes or replies, and no counts.

So, like and reply counts — and threads — are put together by services that index the network, like an AppView or a backlink index. For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts (app.bsky.feed.post/3n2opitxdyc2j), on November 22nd, 2026, public.api.bsky.app mentioned 1951 likes and 774 replies — and so did the Constellation backlink index. (For a recent post, they agree. For older ones, they may not — see the follower counts, below.).

It is one service's opinion. For the same account (reiver.blacksky.team), at the same time (November 22nd, 2026), public.api.bsky.app (Bluesky's AppView) noted 292 followers, api.blacksky.community (the Blacksky team's AppView) said 196, and the Constellation backlink index said 134. (See: ATProto AppView and How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

With enough work, a follower count can be computed exactly.

You would have to check every repository on every PDS — and you can never be sure you found them all, since a relay only knows the hosts it crawls. By the time you finished, the answer would have changed. And, what counts as a follower is a choice — for example, the app.bsky.graph.follow lexicon claims “Duplicate follows will be ignored by the AppView.” (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

A feed generator sends you posts.

In a recent development, it sends a skeleton — a list of post URIs. The AppView fills in the posts. (See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

A label is a signed annotation. What to do with it (hide, blur, warn, nothing) is up to each app and user. (See: ATProto Labeler.).

Account status (active, deactivated, etc) can be verified cryptographically.

It has been revealed that “Unlike other aspects of atproto, account status is not self-certifying”. It is passed along hop by hop — so different services may disagree. When in doubt, ask the account's own PDS (com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus).

Industry observers note that bluesky is one app built on it. Others use their own lexicons — for example, site.standard.document, community.lexicon.calendar.event, and actor.rpg.sprite.

ATProto is a microblogging protocol.

Microblogging (short posts, like Bluesky's) is just one thing built on it. The overview describes ATProto as “a decentralized protocol for large-scale social web applications”. Nothing in the core protocol is about posts — records, repositories, XRPC, and sync work the same for any record type. What a record is comes from its lexicon, and anyone with a domain can define fresh ones.

For example: long-form documents (site.standard.document), calendar events (community.lexicon.calendar.event), game sprites (actor.rpg.sprite), custom feeds (app.bsky.feed.generator), and, in the spaces proposal, bookmarks, private forums, and group chats. Even the protocol's own lexicons are published as records (com.atproto.lexicon.schema).

(Falsehoods that come from comparing ATProto with ActivityPub, the Fediverse, and Mastodon.).

Unlike ActivityPub (and the Fediverse, and Mastodon), ATProto does not use JSON-LD.

In a recent development, DID documents are JSON-LD. plc.directory serves them with the content type application/did+ld+json, and each one starts with an @context:.

(That is from plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz. A did:web document has one too — for example, api.bsky.app/.well-known/did.json.).

Sources indicate that what is true is that ATProto's own data — records, lexicons, XRPC — is not JSON-LD. And, ATProto software usually reads DID documents as plain JSON — the ATProto DID specification notes which fields to read, and does not call for JSON-LD processing.

Like on Mastodon, an ATProto handle includes the user's server — @user@server.

On Mastodon, a user's full address is a user name and a server — Mastodon's documentation says it is “in the form @username@domain”, and that “@user@example.com is not the same as @user@example.org.”.

Industry observers note that an ATProto handle is just one domain name — like reiver.blacksky.team — and it says nothing about the user's server. The server (PDS) is found separately, from the DID document. (A handle shown as @reiver.blacksky.team has just one @, as a decoration.).

ATProto has nothing like a Fediverse “instance”.

According to recent reports, the difference is that it is more hidden. It is not part of the user's identity or handle — reiver.blacksky.team does not say which PDS hosts it. It is not what decides what a user sees — that is mostly the AppView. And, a user can move to another PDS while keeping the same DID, handle, posts, and followers.

Like Mastodon, ATProto looks up handles with WebFinger.

Mastodon uses WebFinger (/.well-known/webfinger) — its documentation states “WebFinger is required for fully interoperating with Mastodon.”.

Industry observers note that ATProto does not. A handle is resolved with a DNS TXT record at _atproto., or with https:///.well-known/atproto-did. (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Like on Mastodon, when a user moves to a new server, their posts stay behind, and their followers have to be moved over.

On Mastodon, moving an account moves followers — but Mastodon's documentation notes “Your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations”, and that “Mastodon presently does not support importing posts or media”. Moving also has to “force everyone to unfollow your current account and follow your new account”.

On ATProto, moving to a fresh PDS includes “migrating data from the old PDS to the new PDS” (from the accounts specification) — the whole repository, posts and all. And, the account keeps the same DID. Since follow records point at the DID, followers do not have to be moved at all. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Like ActivityPub servers, ATProto servers send posts to each other's inboxes.

In ActivityPub, a server pushes each activity to its recipients — the ActivityPub specification describes it being “inserted into the actor's inbox (delivery)”, by HTTP POST.

Like in ActivityPub, to trust a copy of a post, you have to check it against the server it came from.

Sources indicate that the ActivityPub specification indicates servers should do “something at least as robust as checking that the object appears as received at its origin”, and that “No particular mechanism for verification is authoritatively specified”. (Mastodon uses HTTP Signatures, to check who sent an activity.).

It has been revealed that ATProto data checks itself. Repository commits are signed with the account's key, and records are identified by their hash (CID) — so a copy can be checked no matter who it came from. The data model specification states this “makes it possible to redistribute content and trust copies even if coming from an untrusted party.” (See: ATProto Record.).

ATProto and the Fediverse cannot talk to each other.

Sources indicate that they are different protocols — but there are bridges. For example, Bridgy Fed describes itself as “a decentralized social network bridge. It connects the fediverse, the web, and the Atmosphere (Bluesky).” With it, people on one network can follow, reply to, like, and repost people on the other.

(These are about the spaces proposal, which is not yet part of the specification.).

Industry observers note that “Atproto spaces provide access control, not confidentiality. They are not end-to-end encrypted.”.

A space is stored on one server.

Recent findings suggest that each member's records stay on that member's own PDS. “The space does not colocate records on a single network host.”.

A copy of space data proves who wrote it.

Space data is authenticated with MACs, not signatures — on purpose, so that it “should not carry proof of authorship that survives a leak outside its access boundary.”.

Most of these come from the same idea: ATProto separates things that are usually tied together.

So, the safe defaults are: key everything by DID; resolve, do not assume; validate what you read; ignore what you do not understand; and expect other servers to disagree with yours.

Docker patches Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 with Docker Hardened Images

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day.
  • What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application.
  • Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

To decode Base64 promptly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

In a recent development, they demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

It has been revealed that oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

It has been revealed that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

Sources indicate that ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Industry observers note that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check notes otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Industry observers note that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type reveals the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

In a recent development, check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

According to recent reports, ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check says otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Industry observers note that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Industry observers note that check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4.

Fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Recent findings suggest that fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable.

According to recent reports, java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

Sources indicate that not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November update fixes other concerns in these lines, so update when new images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

It has been revealed that they follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Industry observers note that set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the issue, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

In a recent development, the CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

Recent findings suggest that the fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

According to recent reports, A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

According to recent reports, A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

According to recent reports, not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Sources indicate that five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

Sources indicate that A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

Our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

According to recent reports, verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a latest JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Industry observers note that the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

It has been revealed that some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

Pull the fresh image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX concerns that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way.

Recent findings suggest that the Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

According to recent reports, the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and revision this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, notes it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

It has been revealed that if you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how swiftly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

Sources indicate that the Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.
